newsitem.title: UK: Britain opens up its international telecoms market.
newsitem.headline: Britain opens up its international telecoms market.

text.p: Britain on Thursday officially welcomed 44 new international telephone operators to compete for market share, saying it had created a fully open international telecommunications market 12 months ahead of the rest of Europe.

Science and Technology Minister Ian Taylor signed the first new licences for companies to run international services. The new companies can now compete against the dominant giant, British Telecommuncications, and its rival Cable and Wireless's Mercury subsidiary.

"The UK has proved to the world that liberalisation pushes down prices and improves services," Taylor said. "Phone prices are down 40 percent overall since 1984, and I expect these new licensees to put further downward pressure on international rates."

In the largest single move towards opening up the international telecommunications market to competition, 46 companies applied for licences to offer a full range of telecoms services between Britain and the rest of the world. Only 44 licences, effective from January 1, were issed on Thursday.
Until now, companies apart from BT and Mercury have only been able to operate by leasing lines from the two British companies. But own-facilities services are cheaper to provide.

The decision may also help defuse opposition from U.S. telecoms giant AT&T to BT's proposed $20 billion takeover of U.S. phone company MCI Communications. Regulatory clearance hinges on how competitive Britain is deemed to be.
